front: Reasons for applying a surface finish
back: Functional — to improve performance, e.g. corrosion or water resistance. Aesthetic — to improve appearance.
Remove dust, grease and rust; some finishes need the surface keyed (roughened) to grip.
Dry powder applied to metal then cured in an oven — durable and colourful.
Coating steel with zinc to prevent rust.
An electrochemical process that creates a protective oxide layer, commonly on aluminium.
Depositing a thin layer of metal onto a surface, e.g. chrome plating.
Heated metal is dipped into a fluidised bed of polythene powder that melts onto it, then cured — grip, comfort, colour and corrosion protection on tool handles.
Heating mild steel and dipping it in oil, leaving a thin black protective layer.
Changes or enhances the colour of timber; usually sealed with varnish.
A hard, protective coat applied in layers — glossy or matt.
Seals the pores of wood before varnish or polish so fewer coats are needed.
Seals bare wood, especially MDF edges, so paint does not soak in and the top coat sticks.
When the mould surface gives a polymer its finish, so no further finishing is needed.
Draw filing, wet-and-dry paper, polishing compound or flame polishing.
A high-gloss ultraviolet varnish applied to parts of a design, e.g. a business card.
Page edges are glued into the spine of a card cover, as in paperback books.
Holes punched in the pages and held in order by a plastic comb.
